title: Jacques Derrida
summary: Derrida invented “deconstruction” — a slow, attentive kind of reading that shows how every rigid opposition (reason and feeling, strong and weak, one’s own and the stranger’s) is in fact unstable, each side depending on the other. He showed that meaning is never fully “here and now”: it always carries traces of the past and an expectation of the future. In his later work he wrote about mourning, friendship, hospitality and forgiveness — about how to live with others, and with those who are gone.
onEmotions: Derrida never built a theory of emotions, but his concepts give feelings a subtle language. A feeling, like meaning, is never wholly “present”: it always holds a “trace” — a reference to something absent, to what has gone or has not yet arrived. Deconstruction is suspicious of hierarchies in which reason stands “above” feeling and joy is “more correct” than sorrow. And one more important thought: we are bound to other people — living or departed — by relationships that can never be completed, and that incompleteness is not a breakdown but a form of fidelity.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is exhausting, and there is nothing shameful in it. In his essay “Plato’s Pharmacy,” Derrida examines the Greek word pharmakon, which means both “remedy” and “poison.” He shows that many things are built this way: they cannot be split into the purely good and the purely bad. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that anxiety is a kind of pharmakon too. It keeps you from sleeping and breathing, yet there is care in it as well: attention to what might happen, readiness for what matters. You don’t have to declare it your enemy, nor praise it. You can acknowledge its doubleness: “it gets in my way, and it is also looking out for me.” Sometimes that acknowledgment loosens its grip more than any attempt to switch the anxiety off.
anxiety.practice: Finish two sentences: “My anxiety gets in my way by…” and “My anxiety takes care of me by…”.

fear.text: Fear is a natural feeling in the face of what you cannot control. In Specters of Marx, Derrida coined the word “hauntology” — a play on the French hanter, “to haunt.” A ghost is something that seems to be over but keeps coming back, or something that does not yet exist but already disturbs us. Many fears work exactly like this: they come from the past or from a possible future. Derrida suggested not exorcising the ghosts, not pretending they aren’t there, but learning to talk with them and to hear what they ask of us. From this angle you can ask your fear: where have you come from, and what are you trying to tell me? Sometimes a ghost that has been listened to stops being a threat and becomes a messenger.
fear.practice: If your fear were a ghost, where would it have come from — the past or a possible future? What is it trying to tell you?

sadness.text: Sadness is a legitimate feeling, and it needs no justification. Derrida showed that Western thought loves to build pairs — reason and feeling, strength and weakness, joy and sorrow — in which one half counts as “higher.” Deconstruction shows that the “lower” half is not simply subordinate but necessary to the first, and that the border between them is unstable. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that sadness is not a malfunction of some “normal” joyful state but part of the very fabric of feeling. Derrida also coined the word différance: it sounds like the French word for “difference” but is spelled with an “a,” and it means both “differing” and “deferring.” Meaning is never wholly here. Sadness is often about exactly this: about what points toward something absent.
sadness.practice: Write the word “sadness,” and next to it, what it points to: which person, which place, what never came to be. Simply trace the references.

grief.text: Grief is one of the heaviest experiences there is, and it has no correct timeline. Derrida wrote a great deal about mourning: The Work of Mourning gathers his farewell texts for friends who had died — Barthes, Foucault, Deleuze, Levinas and others. He argued against the idea of a “successful” mourning, after which the departed is fully “digested” and let go. Such success, Derrida thought, would in a sense be a betrayal. Fidelity to the one who is gone means keeping them as other, without appropriating them or dissolving them into yourself — and that can never be fully finished. One of his last books is titled Each Time Unique, the End of the World: the death of another is not an event in the world but the end of a whole world. Your grief is proportionate to that, and it doesn’t need to be hurried.
grief.practice: What in you still speaks in the voice of the one who is gone — a phrase, a gesture, an intonation? Let that voice stay, without trying to “close” it.

loneliness.text: Loneliness hurts, and your need for closeness is real. Derrida’s Politics of Friendship opens with an enigmatic sentence that since antiquity has been attributed to Aristotle: “O my friends, there is no friend.” Derrida spends the whole book untangling this paradox. Friendship, in his view, always includes distance and asymmetry: even the closest person remains “wholly other,” with something in them you can never reach. From this angle, loneliness is not just a failure of friendship but its secret part: we address friends who are not yet beside us, those who may still come. This doesn’t cancel the longing, but it makes it less a verdict and more an address — one that may still find an answer.
loneliness.practice: Write a few lines to a friend you haven’t met yet, or lost long ago. There is no need to send them.

quote.text: O my friends, there is no friend.
quote.author: Aristotle (a saying as reported by Diogenes Laertius and Montaigne)
quote.source: The leitmotif of Derrida’s Politics of Friendship (1994)

anger.text: Anger often speaks of a sense of injustice, and that is an important signal. In “Force of Law,” Derrida distinguishes law from justice. Law is statutes, rules, procedures; they can be analyzed, criticized, changed. Justice is something more: it is always addressed to a single person in a singular situation, it is never fully embodied, it is always “to come.” From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that anger often flares in the gap between how things are arranged by the rules and what would be just. That gap is real, and your anger is not a whim. But justice, for Derrida, demands attention to the singularity of each person — including the one you are angry with. Anger can become the voice of justice as long as it doesn’t turn into a new rule with no exceptions.
anger.practice: Put it into words: what justice, not yet realized, stands behind your anger? What would it look like in this particular situation?

shame.text: Shame is a heavy and deeply human feeling. One of Derrida’s late lectures, “The Animal That Therefore I Am,” opens with an unexpected scene: the philosopher stands naked, his cat looks at him, and he feels ashamed — and then ashamed of being ashamed in front of a cat. From this almost comic scene he draws a deep question: who is looking at me, and why do I feel I must hide something? The gaze of the other, Derrida says, can never be appropriated or fully understood. From this angle, shame is a sign that you are open to another’s gaze, that you are not sealed off in yourself. Instead of fleeing shame, you can ask carefully: whose gaze is this — and must it be judging?
shame.practice: Notice whose gaze you feel inside your shame. Could that gaze be not a verdict but simply the presence of another — like the cat’s gaze?

guilt.text: Guilt shows that other people matter to you, and the feeling deserves respect. Derrida thought a great deal about forgiveness and arrived at a radical idea: true forgiveness forgives only the unforgivable. If we forgive only what is easy to forgive, that is not forgiveness but exchange: “you repented — I forgave you.” Genuine forgiveness, for Derrida, is unconditional, neither a deal nor therapy; that is why it is almost “impossible” — and yet it happens. From this angle you could say that relief from guilt does not always have to be earned through endless atonement. Derrida distinguished unconditional forgiveness from conditional forgiveness — through apology, repair, conversation — and admitted that we live between the two. The second is available right now, and it is meaningful.
guilt.practice: What one concrete step of conditional forgiveness — an apology, a conversation, a repair — is possible for you now? And what should simply be left to time?

envy.text: Envy is unpleasant, but everyone knows it. In Of Grammatology, Derrida describes the “logic of the supplement” (supplément): an addition that completes something also reveals that there was no fullness there to begin with. More broadly, Derrida criticized the “metaphysics of presence” — the belief that somewhere there exists a full, whole, self-sufficient being. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that envy lives on exactly this belief: that the other has a fullness I lack. Deconstruction gently takes this picture apart: no one has fullness; every life is shot through with absence, deferral, lack. This doesn’t devalue what you want. But it lets you see that the person you envy also lives with incompleteness, perhaps invisible to you.
envy.practice: Describe the “fullness” you attribute to the person you envy. And who might see that same “fullness” in you?

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy can be very heavy, and feeling them is not your fault. Derrida criticized the dream of a full, immediate meaning that would be wholly “here and now.” Meaning, in his view, always lives in a web of references: every word carries “traces” of other words, every experience points to others. The absence of fullness is not a breakdown but the condition of any meaning. Derrida even valued the gap, the interval — what he called “spacing”: without the blank space between letters, writing would be impossible. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that emptiness is not necessarily “nothing” but a pause in the text of a life. You don’t have to force yourself to feel; it is enough to notice the traces that still point to something.
emptiness.practice: Look around: what one thing, word or habit still points you toward something dear? You don’t need to feel anything — just notice that reference.

quote.text: There is nothing outside of the text.
quote.author: Jacques Derrida

confusion.text: Confusion is natural when there is no obvious path in front of you. Derrida spoke often of “aporia” — Greek for, literally, “no passage,” a dead end. He believed that a real decision is possible only through “the ordeal of the undecidable.” If everything is clear and calculable, that is not a decision but simply the application of a rule, like a calculator. You can truly decide only where you don’t know in advance what is right. From Derrida’s point of view, confusion is not stupidity or weakness but honesty before a genuinely difficult situation in which two truths collide. It means you are not substituting a ready-made formula for a decision. You can bear it without rushing — and when the decision comes, it will truly be yours.
confusion.practice: Write down the two truths you are stuck between, without trying to choose right away. Just let both of them exist on the same page.

fatigue.text: Fatigue and burnout are a real limit, not a weakness of character. Derrida wrote about unconditional hospitality — opening the door to any newcomer without asking their name or setting conditions. But he honestly admitted that in its pure form it is impossible: in real life hospitality needs conditions — a home, doors, rules, time. We always live between the unconditional ideal and the conditions without which it cannot be realized. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that burnout often comes when we try to live the unconditional without conditions: to be endlessly available, to answer everyone, to take everything in. Conditions — a door closed for the evening, a “not now” — are not a betrayal of your ideals but what allows them to go on living.
fatigue.practice: What one “condition of hospitality” — a time when you are unavailable, a simple “not now” — can you set this week?

boredom.text: Boredom is an honest feeling: it seems everything has already been seen and nothing is happening. Derrida was a master of reading in the margins: he carefully examined footnotes, asides, small details that others skipped. In Spurs he devoted a meditation to a phrase found among Nietzsche’s papers — “I have forgotten my umbrella” — and showed how hard it is to decide once and for all what it means. Deconstruction as a whole begins with noticing the unnoticed. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that boredom often arises when we read life only by its “main text,” its familiar plot. The margins — small things, accidents, oddities — are full of meanings waiting for attention.
boredom.practice: Find a “marginalia” of your day — a small thing you usually don’t notice: a crack, a word, a sound. Stay with it for a minute.

joy.text: Joy is a precious feeling, and it doesn’t need to be justified. Derrida was often taken for a skeptic who takes everything apart, but he himself insisted that deconstruction is above all affirmation, a “yes.” In his writings on Joyce he reflected on the double “yes, yes”: the first “yes” is said to life, the second confirms it, repeats it, promises to keep that assent. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that joy is that first “yes,” and the way to cherish it is the second: to remember, to repeat, to confirm. Joy in Derrida is not naive: it knows about fragility and finitude. But that is exactly why it is precious. You don’t have to hide it for fear it will end; you can affirm it twice.
joy.practice: Say a second “yes” to your joy: write it down so that a year from now you can remember it and confirm it again.

love.text: Love and tenderness are among the most important experiences, even when they are hard to explain. In the documentary Derrida (2002), the philosopher is asked about love, and he speaks of the difference between “who” and “what.” Do we love a person — their singularity, a “someone” — or their qualities, a “something”: beauty, intelligence, kindness? Derrida admits that this distinction is never finally settled: love keeps wavering between the two. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that tenderness doesn’t have to answer the question “what for.” Qualities can change and disappear, but what we love in a person as singular slips away from any list. And that is not love’s weakness but its secret.
love.practice: Try to describe someone you love without naming a single one of their qualities — only as a singular person, like no one else.

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm feeling, full of life. In Given Time, Derrida reflects on the gift and arrives at a paradox: a true gift is almost impossible. As soon as a gift is recognized as a gift, it enters an economy of exchange: the one who receives feels indebted, the one who gives expects something back. The circle of “given — returned” cancels the very gratuitousness of the gift. Derrida does not call on us to stop being grateful. From his way of thinking, you could say that the deepest gratitude is the kind that is in no hurry to pay off, that doesn’t turn a gift into a debt. It simply acknowledges: I was given something I could not have earned. And that acknowledgment is enough — with no obligation to return something of equal value right away.
gratitude.practice: Remember a gift you cannot and need not “return.” Let it remain a gift — simply name it to yourself.

hope.text: Hope is a precious feeling, even when it is quiet. Derrida distinguished two French words for the future: futur — the future that can be predicted and planned — and avenir, literally “what is coming,” the unexpected, the unforeseeable. In Specters of Marx he speaks of “messianicity without messianism”: an openness to what is to come without the promise of a particular savior or a ready-made picture of paradise. From Derrida’s point of view, hope is not the certainty that everything will be fine but a preserved openness: a door left ajar for whatever may arrive. Derrida himself, in saying farewell, asked that words affirming life be passed on to those who came to his funeral. Hope, in this sense, is choosing life again and again.
hope.practice: Leave “the door ajar”: write down one thing you cannot predict but would like to meet if it comes.

quote.text: Always prefer life and constantly affirm survival.
quote.author: Jacques Derrida
quote.source: Farewell words read at his funeral (2004)

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a warm, aching feeling, and it speaks of what is dear to you. Derrida knew it well: he grew up in Algeria and all his life spoke of his complicated bond with his childhood and his language. In Monolingualism of the Other he writes that he has only one language, and it does not belong to him. In an early essay, “Structure, Sign, and Play,” Derrida described two attitudes toward a lost origin: a sad, nostalgic one — longing for a lost center — and an affirmative, joyful acceptance that there never was a center and that the world is open to play. He did not demand that we choose one. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that nostalgia loves what was never wholly “ours” — and so it can live alongside openness to the new.
nostalgia.practice: What from the past that you miss was never fully “yours” — and still became part of you?

quote.text: I have only one language; it is not mine.
quote.author: Jacques Derrida

craving.text: Craving — a sharp “I want it right now” — can be very strong, and it doesn’t make you a bad person. In “Plato’s Pharmacy,” Derrida examines the Greek word pharmakon: it means both “remedy” and “poison.” And in the interview “The Rhetoric of Drugs” (1989) he shows that the very notion of a “drug” is not purely medical: it mixes morality, politics, and a fear of the “artificial.” He called neither for praise nor for simple condemnation — he proposed thinking slowly. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that the object of craving — a substance, a cigarette, a phone — works like a pharmakon: it promises relief and at the same time drains your strength. Craving shouts only about the “remedy.” You can calmly remember the other half of the word.
craving.practice: When a craving rises, finish two lines: “Right now this promises me…” and “Afterward it usually takes from me…”. Wait for the wave to ease a little.

addiction.text: Addiction — a long-running circle in which life gradually arranges itself around one thing — is not a moral failure. In “The Rhetoric of Drugs,” Derrida notes that addicts are often condemned for “escaping reality” into an artificial world, and he shows that behind this condemnation stand old philosophical oppositions: “natural — artificial,” “authentic — fake.” Earlier still, in Of Grammatology, he analyzed Rousseau’s expression “dangerous supplement”: something added to life to make up for a lack, which gradually begins to replace it. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that addiction is a supplement that has taken up too much room. The useful question is not “why am I like this” but “what exactly is this making up for?” — loneliness, pain, emptiness, exhaustion.
addiction.practice: Finish the sentence: “For me, this makes up for…” If you want, you can share that answer with someone who understands — for example, in a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: The morning after — heaviness in the body, anxiety, shame, gaps in memory. All of it is agonizing, and you deserve gentleness. Derrida thought a lot about memory as an “archive.” In Archive Fever he shows that an archive is always incomplete, full of losses and erasures, and that the drive to restore everything down to the last detail can itself turn into a fever. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that the morning attempt to reconstruct yesterday minute by minute is also archive fever: anxiety demands a complete record that will never exist. The past only ever reaches us as traces. You can acknowledge these gaps instead of filling them with the worst guesses, and, if needed, calmly ask people you trust — once you feel better.
hangover.practice: Divide a page into two columns: what you definitely remember — and what anxiety is filling in. You don’t have to reread the second column for now.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria — a sudden high when everything seems possible — is a real experience, and you can treasure it. All his life Derrida analyzed the dream of “full presence” — of the moment when everything is finally here, whole, with nothing left over. He showed that any presence is always already shot through with “traces” of past and future. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that euphoria is a rare moment when the dream of fullness feels almost fulfilled. That is no reason to debunk it. But it helps to remember the trace: this moment is precious not because it lasts forever but because it is already leaving an imprint in you, one you will be able to return to. Joy doesn’t have to last forever to be real.
euphoria.practice: Write down one detail of this moment — a sound, a phrase, a color — so that it leaves a trace you can return to.

crash.text: A sharp drop after a high — a celebration, a success, a substance — can feel like falling into a void. It is an understandable reaction, and it isn’t your fault. Derrida wrote a great deal about mourning, and from his thought you can draw the idea that we mourn not only people: any loss — of a place, a time, a state — needs its own work of farewell. From this angle, the comedown is a small mourning for the high that has passed. You don’t have to rush it or hide it. Derrida also coined the word différance, which fuses “difference” and “deferral”: meaning is never given all at once, it keeps being put off. Perhaps what felt complete at the peak will reveal its meaning later, in a calmer state. The drop doesn’t have to pass judgment on what was.
crash.practice: Say goodbye to the high in one sentence: “Thank you for…, I’m sorry it’s over.” Then name one simple thing that will support you today.

panic.text: Panic — a wave of terror, a pounding heart, the sense that something irreparable is about to happen — is one of the most frightening experiences there is. You really are scared. Derrida distinguished two futures: futur — the predictable, the planned — and avenir — what arrives suddenly, without warning. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that panic is an encounter with the unexpected that comes not from outside but from within your own body. The thought “I’m about to lose my mind” is an attempt to read this wave at once as a final text. But Derrida taught us not to rush to a final reading. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. While it passes, you don’t need to interpret it — it is enough to lean on what is there: the floor, your breath, the objects around you.
panic.practice: Press your feet into the floor and take a few slow breaths out, longer than the breath in. Name five objects around you out loud — just name them, without interpreting.

dread.text: Existential dread — “what is it all for,” finitude, the abyss — is a heavy feeling, and very many people know it. Derrida did not hide from these questions. In Aporias he reflected that finitude cannot be “passed through” and fully understood: it remains an “aporia” — in Greek, “no way through.” And in his last interview, Learning to Live Finally, he speaks of “survival” (survivance) — not as something after life, but as life at its most intense, most alive, always bound up with others and with what we pass on to them: traces, words, care. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that the abyss is not an answer but a place from which you can see especially clearly how precious life and our bonds with others are.
dread.practice: Name one trace of you that already remains in other people’s lives: a word, a habit, an act of care. Write it down.

fomo.text: The fear of missing out — the feeling that real life is happening somewhere else, to other people — is familiar to a great many people today. All his life Derrida criticized what he called the “metaphysics of presence”: the conviction that somewhere there exists a full, authentic meaning, life “as it really is,” without gaps or deferrals. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that FOMO is this metaphysics transferred to the feed: for others, life is fully present; for me, there are only traces. But their fullness is an effect too: snapshots, selected and arranged like any text. No one lives in full presence. Knowing this doesn’t devalue your life — it frees it from comparison with something that doesn’t exist.
fomo.practice: Pick one of someone else’s “perfect” pictures and ask: what was left out of the frame? Then name one moment of your day that appeared in no feed at all.

sleepless.text: Insomnia and 3 a.m. thoughts are exhausting: the mind runs through options, weighs, calculates — and can’t stop. In “Force of Law,” Derrida distinguishes calculation from decision. A calculation can be carried to the end if there is enough data. But a real decision, in his view, always passes through “the undecidable” — a moment when no knowledge guarantees the right answer; he even cites Kierkegaard’s words that the instant of decision is a madness. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that the nighttime mind is trying to calculate what cannot be calculated — to go through every option until the risk disappears. That is impossible not because of your weakness but because of the very nature of decisions. So at night you can stop calculating: morning won’t bring a full guarantee, but it will bring more strength.
sleepless.practice: Write down the question that keeps circling, and under it: “This can’t be solved by calculation. I’ll come back to it in the daytime.” Then bring your attention back to your breathing.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply: what breaks is not only a bond but your trust in the world. Your pain is legitimate. Derrida thought a lot about the promise and showed that it is built paradoxically: to be a real promise rather than a mechanical calculation, it must be capable of not being kept. The possibility of breaking it is written into its very structure — otherwise it would be not a promise but a forecast. This does not excuse the person who broke their word. But it explains why trust is always risky: to trust means opening yourself to someone who is truly other and cannot be controlled. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that your trust was not naivety. It was courage, without which no bond is possible — and that courage remains yours.
betrayal.practice: Write: “I trusted because…” — and note what that reason says that is good about you.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is agonizing: every sign, glance, or delayed reply turns into a riddle that can never be fully solved. In The Post Card, Derrida argues with the psychoanalyst Lacan, who claimed that a letter always arrives at its destination. Derrida answers: a letter can always fail to arrive — get lost, reach the wrong person, be understood differently. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that jealousy is a painful encounter with this “undecidability”: another person’s signs never give a full guarantee; they can always be read in different ways. This is not something abnormal in you but the condition of loving a living, separate person. Relief may come not from a final decoding but from accepting that there won’t be one — and from a direct, honest conversation instead of interpretation.
jealousy.practice: Choose one sign that troubles you and write three different readings of it, not just one. Notice that you don’t know which of them is true.

resentment.text: An old grudge — something you carry with you for years — is heavy, and it speaks of a real wound. Derrida wrote a great deal about forgiveness and insisted on something unexpected: true forgiveness cannot be an obligation. If it is demanded, bought with apologies, turned into a procedure of “reconciliation,” it stops being forgiveness and becomes a deal. Forgiveness, for Derrida, is an unconditional gift, possible only as something exceptional. From this angle, you are not obliged to forgive on schedule, and your grudge is not a moral failure. But holding on to it is not a duty either. Between “forgive” and “never forgive” there is a space: to acknowledge the wound, to remember it — and yet gradually stop giving it the central place in your life.
resentment.practice: Write: “I don’t need to forgive right now. But I can let this grudge take up a little less room, for example…” — and add one concrete thing.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart hurts almost physically: the person is alive but has left your life, and that is a loss of its own particular kind. For Derrida, any relationship with another carries the possibility of separation from the very beginning: we are bound to the other precisely as someone separate, someone who can leave. The first part of his book The Post Card, “Envois,” is written as love letters full of distance and uncertainty. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that a breakup does not cancel what was: the relationship leaves a “trace” that goes on living in you — in words, habits, ways of seeing. You don’t need to erase that trace by force or keep it as a shrine. You can allow yourself sadness and allow the other to remain other — not possessed, but not crossed out either.
heartbreak.practice: Name one trace of this relationship that you would like to keep in yourself: a word, a habit, a way of seeing things. It is yours, even though the person has gone.

impostor.text: The fear that you are about to be exposed as “not the real thing” is familiar to many, and more often it speaks of how demanding you are of yourself than of any actual fakery. In the essay “Signature Event Context,” Derrida shows something curious: a signature, the most personal mark of authenticity, works only because it can be repeated. All authenticity rests on repetition, imitation, citation. Each of us learns to speak, write and work by repeating others — what Derrida called “iterability.” From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that the inner “impostor” starts from a myth of the pure original — of people who “truly” know how to do everything on their own. There are no such people. Relying on what you have learned from others is not deception but the condition of any skill.
impostor.practice: Name three people from whom you learned something for your work. Notice: relying on other people’s experience is not imposture but the ordinary path.

self_hatred.text: Self-hatred and a merciless inner critic are a very heavy experience, and that voice does not tell the truth about you. In his late work Derrida used the biological concept of “autoimmunity”: the case in which the body’s defense system begins to attack the body itself. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that the inner critic resembles such a mechanism: once, perhaps, it was meant to protect you from mistakes, rejection, shame, but now it strikes at what it should be protecting. Deconstruction also teaches distrust of rigid oppositions: “worthy — worthless,” “strong — weak.” The critic speaks in exactly such binary verdicts. Instead of refuting them on the spot, you can notice that they are too simple for a living person.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one of the critic’s phrases and ask: “What was this voice once trying to protect me from?” Answer it the way you would answer a close friend.

helplessness.text: Helplessness — the sense that you can’t change anything — is heavy, and it often reflects real circumstances rather than your weakness. Derrida had an unusual relationship with “the impossible.” Forgiveness, the gift, hospitality, justice are, in his view, impossible in the full sense: a pure gift must expect nothing in return, true justice cannot be reduced to a rule. But it is precisely in this “experience of the impossible” that he saw the place where responsibility begins, not where it ends. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say: the fact that you can’t solve everything doesn’t make your small responses meaningless. Helplessness is not a verdict on your strength but an encounter with its limit; and right at that limit you can still respond — with attention, a word, your presence.
helplessness.practice: Write: “I can’t…” and next to it: “But I can respond to this by…” — one smallest possible action.

procrastination.text: “I can’t get started” is a familiar and draining state, and it isn’t laziness. Derrida coined the word différance: in French it sounds exactly like différence, “difference,” but it also carries the sense of “putting off.” Meaning, for Derrida, is always deferred: it is never given at once and in full. From this angle you could say that there is never a full, ready-made meaning at the start of any work — and putting things off is often fed by the expectation that you can begin only once everything is clear. In Dissemination, Derrida ironically examines prefaces: they are written last, even though they are placed first. So you don’t have to start at the beginning — clarity will come as you work.
procrastination.practice: Write a draft “not from the beginning”: any piece of the task, deliberately imperfect, for five minutes. The preface can come later.

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home — emigration, a move, losing your ground — is a real loss. Derrida knew it from the inside: he was born in Algeria into a Jewish family and, as a child under the Vichy regime, lost his French citizenship and was expelled from school. Later he wrote Of Hospitality and noted that the French word hôte means both “host” and “guest”: the same people trade places. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that someone who has moved lives in this doubleness: in the new place they are a guest, but gradually they also become a host — of their own corner, language, habits — and one day they welcome others. The feeling of “not quite belonging” is not a flaw but a special knowledge that those who never left don’t have.
uprooted.practice: Recall one thing in which you are already a “host” here — your route, your café, a skill. And one in which you are still a guest. Both positions are legitimate.

overload.text: Overload — the feed, notifications, endless news — is exhausting, and it isn’t a personal weakness. In conversations with the philosopher Bernard Stiegler, published as Echographies of Television, Derrida proposed the word “artifactuality”: “actuality,” the events of the day, doesn’t simply happen — it is made, selected, edited, delivered at a certain rhythm. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that overload is an encounter not with the world as such but with an enormous production of messages about the world, designed for your attention. Derrida didn’t call for turning away from events, but he insisted on slow, critical reading. And slow reading takes time and pause. Switching off the stream for a while is not escape but the condition of attentiveness.
overload.practice: Choose one news item or one post and read it slowly, like a text: who made it, what was selected, what was left out of the frame. Let the rest wait.

unreality.text: The feeling that you or the world around you somehow isn’t real can be strange and frightening. It deserves careful handling, without hasty conclusions. In Voice and Phenomenon, Derrida showed that even the closest thing — the sense “I am here, I hear myself” — is never given to us whole and instantly: it is mediated by signs, memory, a tiny delay. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that full, hundred-percent presence is an ideal, not the norm, and in moments of unreality you simply feel acutely a gap that everyone has. This doesn’t mean the world has vanished. Its traces remain: the weight of objects, sound, touch. You can return to them without demanding that reality be completely solid.
unreality.practice: Touch three different surfaces near you and name them: smooth, warm, rough. These are traces of the world that need no proof.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful — mountains, the sea, a cathedral, the night sky — is a precious feeling, worth simply savoring. In The Truth in Painting, Derrida closely examines Kant’s “sublime” and devotes a chapter to “the colossal” — what is almost too large for our perception. Kant wrote that in such moments the imagination cannot take in the whole, and this is at once unsettling and elevating. Derrida carefully shows that the sublime lives at the border, at the very edge of our capacity to grasp. From this angle, awe is an encounter with the “almost too big” that fits into no frame. You don’t need to explain it or photograph it: you can let it remain a little larger than you are able to hold.
awe.practice: Stand for a minute before whatever stirred your awe, without taking a photo. Notice where your capacity to take it in with your eyes runs out.

relief.text: Relief — when things let go and you can finally breathe out — deserves to be noticed. Derrida loved words with a double bottom. For Hegel’s key concept Aufhebung — “sublation,” in which something is at once cancelled, preserved and raised to a new level — he proposed the French word relève: both “lifting up” and “the changing of the guard.” From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that relief is like such a changing of the guard: the tension doesn’t simply disappear, it hands over its post but leaves experience in you. Now you know that you held out. You don’t need to look for the next worry right away or hurry on. You can let yourself stand in this minute when the guard has changed.
relief.practice: Name in one sentence exactly what you held out through. Take three slow breaths out, noting to yourself: “post handed over.”

calm.text: Calm and peace are not emptiness but a special, open state. It is good simply to be in them. In the essay “Khōra” (1993), Derrida examines an enigmatic word from Plato’s dialogue Timaeus. Khōra is a place, a space that receives everything that appears in it but coincides with none of it, appropriates nothing, holds on to nothing. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that calm resembles khōra: not an absence of thoughts and feelings but the capacity to give them room without clutching at any of them. Everything passes through you, and you remain spacious. Such calm doesn’t have to be earned or used for anything — it is valuable in itself.
calm.practice: Sit for a minute, noticing thoughts and sounds as things passing through a space, and hold on to none of them.

inspiration.text: Inspiration — when something new seems to arrive on its own — is a joyful and somewhat mysterious state. In the essay “Psyche: Invention of the Other,” Derrida plays on the double sense of that phrase: we invent the other, the new, but the other also, as it were, invents us, comes to us from outside. A true invention, in his view, cannot be fully programmed — it is always a bit of a “newcomer,” an unexpected guest. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that inspiration is a visit that cannot be summoned on command but can be met with hospitality. You don’t need to claim it as a personal achievement or fear that it will leave. Better to write down what has come while the guest is here — and leave the door open.
inspiration.practice: Write down everything that has come right now, without editing. At the end add a line: “What else might knock at this door?”

schadenfreude.text: A secret joy when something goes wrong for someone else is familiar to almost everyone, and it doesn’t make you a bad person. In Of Grammatology, Derrida closely reads Rousseau, who considered compassion the most natural, “pure” feeling. Derrida shows that even compassion requires imagination — comparing yourself with another, putting yourself in their place. And where there is comparison, its shadow is always close by. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that schadenfreude and sympathy are not the opposites of a “good” and a “spoiled” heart but two sides of one movement: we measure ourselves against others. Someone else’s failure seems for a moment to confirm your place. Knowing this doesn’t commit you to gloating, but it frees you from shame over the mere fact of the feeling and lets you ask: what comparison is occupying me so strongly right now?
schadenfreude.practice: Finish the sentence: “Their failure for a second made me…” What does that word say about your own insecurity or tiredness?

contempt.text: Contempt is a cold, “looking down” feeling, and it often protects something very vulnerable. Derrida’s deconstruction begins with attention to pairs of concepts in which one is placed above the other: reason and feeling, serious and frivolous, “us” and “them.” He shows that such a hierarchy is held in place by violence: the “lower” term is needed so that the “higher” can define itself at all. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that contempt is a hierarchy built inside the soul: for me to be “normal,” “worthy,” someone has to end up below. Sometimes there is real pain or hurt in this. But it helps to notice how much the “high” depends on the “low.” Then contempt need not be suppressed but can be read: what exactly am I trying so hard to separate from myself?
contempt.practice: Write down which quality in a person arouses your contempt. Then ask: where is that quality — or the fear of it — in me?

disgust.text: Disgust is a strong, almost bodily reaction: you want to pull back, turn away, “spit it out.” It is an ancient protective mechanism, and there is no need to be ashamed of it. In the essay “Economimesis,” Derrida reads Kant’s Critique of Judgment and notices: the one thing Kant does not allow even in art is the disgusting. Everything else can be “digested” into a beautiful image, but the disgusting cannot; it becomes what the system expels in order to stay whole. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that disgust — toward people, a situation, or yourself — marks the border of what you can take in right now. That border is not eternal and doesn’t necessarily say anything about the worth of what is rejected. It is enough to notice it, without turning it into a final verdict on either the other or yourself.
disgust.practice: Notice where in your body the disgust lives. Ask: “What exactly can I not let into myself right now?” — and simply write down the answer.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is understandable: you were hurt, and a sense of injustice inside is demanding an outlet. In Politics of Friendship, Derrida argues with the jurist Carl Schmitt, who held that politics begins with a clear distinction between “friend” and “enemy.” Derrida shows that this border is never final: an enemy may be a former friend, and a friend can wound more deeply than an enemy. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that the thirst for revenge tries to fix the other permanently in the role of enemy — and in doing so chains you to them as well. At the same time, the demand for justice in it is real: what happened must be acknowledged. You can respect that demand without handing it the wheel. A revenge fantasy is a signal of a wound, not a plan of action; hearing the signal is already a step toward getting your freedom back.
revenge.practice: Write what you actually want from the situation: acknowledgment, an apology, safety, distance? Which of these steps requires no one’s pain?

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those closest to you — a partner, parents, children — can be especially sharp, and afterward you feel ashamed of it. But it doesn’t cancel love. Derrida wrote a lot about hospitality and coined the word hostipitalité, “hostipitality”: in Latin hostis (stranger, enemy) and hospes (guest, host) share a root. He shows that hospitality always carries tension: in welcoming another, we give up our space, time, strength to them, and the host sometimes feels like a hostage. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that intimacy is the deepest kind of hospitality, and so flashes of hostility within it are inevitable. Anger here often says: my boundaries have worn thin. You don’t need to pour it out on the other person — you can hear it as a request for room for yourself.
anger_at_loved.practice: Finish the sentence: “When I’m angry at someone close, what I’m missing is…” (quiet, help, recognition, time). Which of these can you give yourself today, even for ten minutes?

ambivalence.text: Loving someone and at the same time being unable to stand them is hard and confusing, but it is a very common and honest state. All his life Derrida worked with what he called the “double bind”: situations in which two opposite demands are equally legitimate and neither cancels the other. He was in no hurry to reconcile them, because a hasty synthesis usually suppresses one side. In one of his last interviews, speaking about himself, he admitted that he was at war with himself. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that mixed feelings toward someone close are not a mistake to be fixed by choosing “I really love them” or “I really hate them.” Both feelings tell the truth about different sides of the bond. You can hold them together without demanding a final verdict of yourself.
ambivalence.practice: Divide a page into two columns: “What I love in them” and “What I can’t stand.” Fill in both without crossing out a single line.

quote.text: I am at war with myself.
quote.author: Jacques Derrida
quote.source: Interview with Le Monde (2004), published under the title “I Am at War with Myself”

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, a departure, or even the death of a seriously ill loved one can be frightening: “how can I feel relieved?” But relief and love can live side by side. Derrida wrote of the “law of friendship”: from their first meeting, each of two friends knows that one of them will most likely outlive the other and mourn them. Loss is written into every bond from the very beginning, and anticipating it becomes part of love itself. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that a long farewell — an illness, a difficult relationship — begins mourning before the end. So relief doesn’t mean there was no love: you may have been carrying both grief and strain for a long time. Relief is not betrayal but the exhale of someone who has held a heavy load for a long time.
guilty_relief.practice: Write one sentence beginning “I feel relieved because…” and a second one — “And I still love/value…”. Keep both.

indifference.text: Sometimes you aren’t moved by what you “should” be: someone else’s grief, a celebration, important news. And guilt about your indifference arrives right away. Derrida coined the word différance (with an “a” instead of an “e”), joining two senses of the French verb différer: “to differ” and “to defer.” Meaning, in his view, is never given at once and in full — it is always late, it comes afterward, through traces. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that feeling, too, doesn’t have to show up on schedule. The lack of a response now doesn’t prove you don’t care: the experience may be deferred, muffled by tiredness or by self-protection, or it may come by another path. The demand “feel the right thing right now” is a program, not a response. Allow yourself not to perform a feeling, and see what comes later.
indifference.practice: Write: “Right now I don’t feel… Perhaps that’s because…” and note what you feel instead, even if it is tiredness or emptiness.

escape.text: The wish to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — and go somewhere no one knows you says that your present life has grown cramped. That is a legitimate signal. In The Post Card, Derrida coined the word destinerrance — from destination (address, destiny) and errance (wandering): any letter may fail to reach its addressee, go astray, end up with someone else. So it is with us: no single role defines us once and for all. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that the wish to run away is your “wandering letter”: part of you doesn’t match the address at which you currently live. This doesn’t require an immediate escape, but it isn’t worth silencing that voice either. You can ask where exactly it is calling you and which “I” in you doesn’t fit into your current role.
escape.practice: Describe in three sentences the place or life you want to run away to. What one quality of that life could you let into your present one, for a while?

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is unavailable or “the wrong person” often brings turmoil and shame. But the feeling itself is not a wrongdoing. In Passions, Derrida speaks a great deal about “the secret”: in every other there is something that is never fully revealed, and it is precisely this inaccessibility that draws us. He insisted that the secret doesn’t need to be exposed or reduced to a simple explanation. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that forbidden attraction shows how desire reaches toward the other precisely as other — toward what cannot be possessed. Perhaps in this person you recognize something you lack: liveliness, freedom, a different life. You don’t need to pass judgment on yourself or rush to a decision. You can treat the secret with respect — your own as well — and ask what this desire is saying.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down three words that describe what draws you to this person. Which of these qualities would you like to develop more in your own life?

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgment is exhausting: every word seems to be sitting an exam. In “Signature Event Context,” Derrida showed that any sign — a word, a gesture, a signature — can be repeated, quoted, and read in a context other than the one its author intended. He called this “iterability.” It follows that no one fully controls how they will be understood. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that social anxiety is a desperate attempt to keep hold of every possible reading of yourself. But that task is impossible for anyone, even the most confident person. There is relief in this: if perception can’t be fully controlled, you can stop trying. Your words will be read in different ways — and that isn’t your mistake, it is how all speech works.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a conversation, tell yourself: “I will be read in different ways, and that’s fine.” Afterward, write down one sentence you said well enough.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is hard: you want to know what will happen, and you can’t. In “Force of Law,” Derrida speaks of “the undecidable” — a situation in which no rule guarantees the right answer. And he draws an unexpected conclusion: only in such a situation is a real decision possible. If everything could be calculated, a decision would simply be the running of a program. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that uncertainty is not a breakdown in your life but the condition for anything in it being decided and happening at all. That doesn’t make it pleasant, but it changes its meaning: you don’t have to know everything in advance in order to act. You can take the next small step, acknowledging that it is taken “at the edge” of knowledge — as are most important steps, for everyone.
uncertainty.practice: Write: “I don’t know how it will turn out. I know that right now I can…” — and name one small step for the coming day.

waiting.text: Waiting — for results, an answer, news — stretches time and keeps you from living in the present. Derrida wrote the essay “Before the Law” on Kafka’s parable: a man comes to the door of the law, the doorkeeper says “not yet,” and the man waits at the door his whole life. At the end he learns that the door was meant for him alone. Derrida reads the parable as a story of how waiting can become one’s entire life if it is given all one’s attention. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that your waiting is legitimate, but it doesn’t have to fill the whole space. The door will open or it won’t, and that is not always in your power. But whether you sit motionless by the door — that, in part, is. You can wait while continuing to live beside the door.
waiting.practice: Choose one activity for the next hour that has nothing to do with what you are waiting for. Tell yourself: “I am waiting — and living at the same time.”

regret.text: Regret over what you did or didn’t do can return again and again, like an intrusive guest. In Specters of Marx, Derrida coined the word “hauntology” — from the French hanter, “to haunt.” The past, in his view, does not vanish without a trace: it returns as ghosts with whom we have to speak. He opens the book with the thought that one can learn to live only in conversation with ghosts. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that regret is such a ghost: a path not taken or a word that can’t be taken back. There is no use driving it out by force, but you can listen to it. Often the ghost comes with a question: what truly matters to you? The answer can become not a verdict on the past but a hint for the future.
regret.practice: Write a letter from the “ghost” of your regret to you: what does it want to tell you about what matters to you now?

longing.text: Longing for a particular person — their voice, their habits, their presence — can be almost physical. In Rams, Derrida closely reads a line by the poet Paul Celan: “The world is gone, I must carry you.” Derrida sees in it the essence of our bond with an other who is not beside us: when the other is far away or gone, we carry them within us — in memory, in words, in a way of seeing the world. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that longing is the very feeling of this burden, its weight. It is heavy, but it also bears witness to the bond: you carry the person because they are dear to you. You don’t need to strive to “stop missing them.” You can notice how exactly you carry them, and let this be a form of fidelity, not only of pain.
longing.practice: Recall one habit, phrase or way of looking at things of this person that lives in you. Do something in their spirit today — small and warm.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — from grim news, wars, injustice — can weigh you down. It speaks of your sensitivity, not your weakness. In The Gift of Death, Derrida reflects on an undecidable paradox of responsibility: in responding to one other, in caring for one, I inevitably fail at that moment to respond to countless others. No one can answer all the pain of the world at once. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that guilt over “insufficient” care for the world is not a sign of your callousness but part of the human condition. It is no reason to turn away, but it is a reason to let go of the demand to be responsible for everything. You can choose one concrete response — attention, help, a word — and recognize that it is meaningful, even if it doesn’t cover everything.
world_pain.practice: Name one concrete thing you can do this week: support someone, help with a deed or a word. Then put the news aside for a minute.

quote.author: Jacques Derrida
quote.source: The Gift of Death (1992); in the French original, “Tout autre est tout autre”

rejection.text: Rejection wounds painfully: it feels as if you have been told “no” entirely, to the whole of you. In the essay “Ulysses Gramophone,” Derrida reflects on the word “yes” — the last word of Joyce’s novel. He shows that a real “yes” is possible only where a “no” is also possible: consent that could not have been withheld is not consent but an automaton. The other’s freedom to refuse is the condition for their “yes” ever meaning anything. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that refusal is a bitter but inseparable side of the other’s freedom, not a verdict on your worth. It speaks of a meeting of two freedoms that, this time, did not coincide. The pain doesn’t disappear, but it stops being proof that something is wrong with you.
rejection.practice: Write: “This person (or place) is free to say ‘no’ to me. This ‘no’ is about them and the situation, not about the whole of me.” Read it aloud.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned can poison even good relationships: you expect someone to leave before there is any reason. This fear often grows out of old wounds and deserves gentleness. In his farewell text Adieu to Emmanuel Levinas, Derrida reflects on the French word adieu. In many places it is used not only to say goodbye but also as a greeting on meeting. That is, every “hello” already holds a “farewell”: meeting another acknowledges from the very start their separateness and freedom. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that your fear senses this truth about every bond acutely. But what follows from it is not only anxiety: since the other is free to leave, their presence beside you is each time a gift, not an obligation. Today they are here, and you can notice that.
abandonment.practice: Note one concrete sign that someone close to you is here today: a message, a gesture, a word. Stay with it for a minute.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love wounds painfully: you give your feeling, and in return there is silence or a polite refusal. In Given Time, Derrida reflects on the gift and arrives at a paradox: a true gift cannot be written into an exchange. As soon as I expect a return, the gift turns into a deal. A gift in the strict sense is what is given without demanding anything back. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that your love, left unanswered, is not a failed deal but perhaps the closest thing to a gift there is. This doesn’t cancel the pain or the wish for reciprocity, and you don’t need to give those up. But you can see that the feeling you experienced has value in itself, not only as an investment that ought to pay off.
unrequited.practice: Write down what this love taught you about yourself: what you are capable of feeling, noticing, giving.

humiliation.text: Humiliation is one of the most painful experiences: as if you had been reduced to something small and worthless and put on display. In Of Grammatology, Derrida speaks of the “originary violence” of naming: any name, label, classification already cuts a person out of their complexity and pins them in place. Humiliation is an extreme form of this violence: another tries to fix a single definition to you — “pathetic,” “ridiculous,” “nobody.” From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that such a definition is never the last word. Meaning, he said, always escapes final fixing; all the more so a person. A humiliating scene is one text about you, read by one reader — not the whole truth. You are still more than what you were called.
humiliation.practice: Write down the label that was pinned on you. Next to it write three other facts about yourself that this label cannot contain.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body can be quiet and constant, and it deserves not criticism but gentleness. Derrida curated an exhibition at the Louvre and wrote the book Memoirs of the Blind — about drawings and self-portraits. He noticed something strange: when drawing themselves, artists cannot look at themselves and at the page at the same time, so every self-portrait is partly drawn blind. We never see ourselves whole and directly — only in a mirror, in a photo, through other people’s eyes. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that your image of your body is a self-portrait too, drawn partly blind, dictated by other people’s gazes and pictures. It doesn’t coincide with the living body that breathes, feels, and holds you in the world. You can trust this portrait a little less — and the body itself a little more.
body_shame.practice: Close your eyes and describe your body not by how it looks but by how it feels: warmth, breath, support, the touch of your clothes. What is it doing for you right now?

illness.text: When illness lets your body down, it is hard both physically and emotionally: plans collapse, you have to depend on others. Derrida gave his last major interview, Learning to Live Finally, when he was already seriously ill. He spoke of “survival” (survie) — and insisted that this is not a pitiful remnant of life but life itself in its intense, most living form: to live is always to live “beyond,” in spite of. He admitted that he had never learned how to live, and he kept on learning. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that a time of illness is not a pause in “real” life but life too, with its own discoveries, bonds and affirmations. You don’t need to put on a show of cheerfulness. But each day still holds something you can affirm: a conversation, a taste, a thought, someone’s hand.
illness.practice: Write down one thing you would like to affirm today: a small pleasure, a conversation, a thought. Let it be your “yes” to this day.

pride.text: Pride in what you have done is a healthy and deserved feeling; let yourself enjoy it. In Otobiographies, reading Nietzsche, Derrida says something unexpected: the final signature on a text is set not by the author but by “the ear of the other” — the one who has heard and received what was said. What we make comes alive when someone responds to it, “countersigns” it. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that pride is doubly good when you notice both signatures: your own — effort, courage, work — and those of the people who received it, helped, and rejoiced with you. This doesn’t diminish your achievement but makes it alive and shared. Pride doesn’t have to be modest or solitary: you can celebrate it, recognizing both yourself and those beside you.
pride.practice: Say out loud what exactly you have done. Then remember one person who responded to it — and perhaps tell them so.

melancholy.text: Bright sadness, melancholy, is a quiet, deep feeling in which there is no misfortune, only tenderness toward what is gone and fragile. It doesn’t need to be “cured.” For many years Derrida kept returning to one phrase: Il y a là cendre — “cinders there are.” In the small book Cinders (Feu la cendre, 1987) he reflects on ash as the most fragile of traces: of what was, almost nothing remains, and yet this “almost nothing” is here, and it can be noticed. From Derrida’s point of view, you could say that melancholy is attention to such traces: the smell of autumn, an old photograph, time gone by. It doesn’t demand the return of the past, nor does it seek to forget it. It is a way of keeping what no longer exists with a light touch — and there is a beauty of its own in that.
melancholy.practice: Find some “cinders” around you — a small trace of the past: an object, a smell, a sound. Sit with it for a minute, doing nothing.
